entries.1:1: This introduces Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, and lists his family line. It reminds the reader that this story is about a real, ordinary family with a history.
entries.1:2: Elkanah had two wives, and one of them, Peninnah, had children while Hannah had none. In that culture, having no children was a deep sorrow, so this sets up Hannah's pain.
entries.1:3: Elkanah faithfully went to Shiloh each year to worship and offer sacrifices to God, where Eli's sons served as priests. It shows his devotion, but also hints that the priesthood there had problems.
entries.1:4: When Elkanah offered his sacrifice, he shared the meat with Peninnah and all her children. This was a joyful family meal connected to worship.
entries.1:5: Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her, even though God had not given her children. His love did not erase her sorrow, but he showed her kindness.
entries.1:6: Peninnah deliberately provoked Hannah to make her miserable about being childless. It shows how one person's cruelty can deepen another's grief.
entries.1:7: This happened year after year, and Peninnah's taunting at worship time left Hannah weeping and unable to eat. The place meant for worship became a place of pain for her.
entries.1:8: Elkanah asked Hannah why she was crying and reminded her that he loved her more than many sons could. He meant well, but his words could not fully heal her longing.
entries.1:9: After the family meal at Shiloh, Hannah got up while Eli the priest was sitting by the doorway of the Lord's temple. The scene shifts to her private moment with God.
entries.1:10: Deeply grieved and crying, Hannah poured out her prayer to the Lord. She brought her pain honestly to God rather than hiding it.
entries.1:11: Hannah made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to the Lord for life as a Nazirite. She was willing to give back to God what she most longed for.
entries.1:12: Hannah prayed for a long time, and Eli watched her mouth. Her long prayer drew the attention of the priest.
entries.1:13: Hannah was praying silently from her heart, with only her lips moving, so Eli assumed she was drunk. He misread her deep devotion as misbehavior.
entries.1:14: Eli told her to sober up and put away her wine. He judged her wrongly without knowing what was really happening.
entries.1:15: Hannah respectfully explained that she was not drunk but was pouring out her broken heart to the Lord. She defended herself calmly and honestly.
entries.1:16: She asked Eli not to think of her as a worthless woman, since her words came from great sorrow and pain. She wanted to be understood rather than condemned.
entries.1:17: Eli blessed her and prayed that Israel's God would grant her request. His words turned from accusation to encouragement.
entries.1:18: Hannah accepted his blessing, went back to eat, and her face was no longer sad. The priest's kindness and her trust in God lifted her spirits.
entries.1:19: The family worshiped early in the morning and returned home, and God remembered Hannah. The phrase means God acted on her behalf at the right time.
entries.1:20: Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son, naming him Samuel because she had asked the Lord for him. The name reflects her prayer being answered.
entries.1:21: Elkanah went up with his family for the yearly sacrifice and to keep his vow. He continued his regular pattern of worship.
entries.1:22: Hannah chose to stay home until the child was weaned, then planned to bring him to the Lord permanently. She took her vow seriously and waited for the right time.
entries.1:23: Elkanah agreed to let her wait until the child was weaned and encouraged her to keep her promise to God. He supported her decision rather than pressuring her.
entries.1:24: Once Samuel was weaned, Hannah brought him to Shiloh with an ox, flour, and wine for sacrifice. She came prepared to fulfill her vow.
entries.1:25: After offering the ox, they brought the young child to Eli the priest. The moment of dedication had arrived.
entries.1:26: Hannah reminded Eli that she was the woman he had seen praying there before. She connected her present joy to that earlier painful moment.
entries.1:27: She explained that this child was the answer to her prayer. She gave God the credit for what she had asked and received.
entries.1:28: Hannah gave Samuel to the Lord for his whole life, and they worshiped there. Her gift back to God came from gratitude for the gift he had given her.
entries.2:1: Hannah is praying out of deep joy because God answered her prayer and helped her. It means you can be honest and glad before God when he lifts you up, even if others opposed you.
entries.2:2: Hannah says there is no one and nothing like God—he alone is holy and completely reliable. It means you can trust God as a solid rock when everything else feels shaky.
entries.2:3: She warns people to stop bragging and talking big, because God knows everything and judges what people do. It means watch your proud words, since God sees and weighs your actions.
entries.2:4: God can break the power of strong warriors and give strength to the weak. It means human strength is not what decides things—God can reverse who is strong and who is not.
entries.2:5: People who had plenty can end up begging, while the needy find rest, and a childless woman can become a mother of many. It means God can turn around anyone's situation, so don't assume things will stay as they are.
entries.2:6: God is the one who decides life and death, bringing people down to the grave and raising them up. It means your life and death are in God's hands, not just chance.
entries.2:7: God gives wealth and can take it away, and he can bring people low or lift them high. It means don't put your security in money, since God is the one who really controls it.
entries.2:8: God lifts the poor and needy from the dust and gives them a place of honor with rulers. It means no one is too low for God to raise up and treat with dignity.
entries.2:9: God protects the steps of those who belong to him, but wicked people will be silenced in darkness, because strength alone won't save anyone. It means you can rely on God's protection rather than your own power.
entries.2:10: Those who fight against God will be shattered, and God will judge the whole earth and strengthen his chosen king. It means opposing God is a losing battle, and he is the final judge over everyone.
entries.2:11: Elkanah goes home to Ramah, and young Samuel stays to serve the Lord under the priest Eli. It means Samuel's life of service began early, showing that even a child can be given to God's work.
entries.2:12: Eli's sons were wicked men who had no real knowledge of the Lord. It means being religious by position doesn't mean knowing God—character matters more than role.
entries.2:13: The priests had a custom of sending a servant with a three-pronged hook to take meat from people's offerings. It means the priests were taking what was meant for worship, which sets up the problem of greed.
entries.2:14: Whatever meat came up on the hook, the priest's servant took for the priests, and this happened to everyone bringing offerings at Shiloh. It means the priests were grabbing their share in a way that treated people's offerings as fair game.
entries.2:15: Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant demanded raw meat for the priest instead of the boiled portion. It means they were greedy and disrespectful of how God's offerings were supposed to work.
entries.2:16: If the worshiper asked them to burn the fat first, the servant refused and threatened to take the meat by force. It means the priests were bullying people and ignoring God's rules for worship.
entries.2:17: The sin of these young men was very serious before the Lord because they treated his offerings with contempt. It means disrespecting God in worship is not a small thing—it is serious in his eyes.
entries.2:18: Samuel, still a child, served in the Lord's house wearing a linen ephod. It means even a young person can faithfully serve God, and his example stands out against the corruption around him.
entries.2:19: His mother made him a small robe and brought it each year when she came with her husband for the annual offering. It means small, faithful acts of care can support someone's service to God year after year.
entries.2:20: Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, asking God to give them children in place of the son they gave to the Lord. It means God honors those who give sacrificially, and blessing can come through faithful priests.
entries.2:21: God showed mercy to Hannah and she had three more sons and two daughters, while Samuel grew up before the Lord. It means God can restore what was given up, and he was watching over Samuel's growth.
entries.2:22: Eli was very old and kept hearing reports of what his sons were doing to all Israel. It means a leader's failure to stop wrongdoing eventually becomes known and affects everyone.
entries.2:23: Eli confronted his sons, asking why they were doing these things, since he heard about their evil from all the people. It means it's right to confront wrongdoing, though words alone aren't enough.
entries.2:24: Eli told his sons that the reports spreading among the Lord's people were not good. It means a bad reputation among God's people is a serious warning sign that something is deeply wrong.
entries.2:25: Eli said that if someone sins against another person, God can judge it, but sinning against the Lord is far worse—yet his sons wouldn't listen, because God had decided to bring them down. It means ignoring correction hardens you, and sin against God is the most serious kind.
entries.2:26: Young Samuel grew and was liked by both the Lord and people. It means a life that pleases God also tends to earn the respect of others.
entries.2:27: A man of God came to Eli and reminded him that the Lord had revealed himself to his ancestors when they were slaves in Egypt. It means God's past faithfulness makes it worse when his chosen servants betray him.
entries.2:28: God says he chose Eli's ancestors from all the tribes to be priests, to serve at the altar and wear the ephod, and he gave them the offerings of Israel. It means Eli's family had been given a great privilege, which made their failure more serious.
entries.2:29: God asks why Eli treated his offerings with contempt by honoring his sons above God and fattening himself on the best parts of Israel's offerings. It means putting family above God and profiting from worship is a serious betrayal.
entries.2:30: God had promised Eli's family a lasting place before him, but now says that will not happen—he honors those who honor him and treats with contempt those who despise him. It means God's promises don't excuse disobedience, and honoring him is what really matters.
entries.2:31: God says the time is coming when Eli's strength and his family's strength will be cut off. It means a family that abuses a sacred role will lose the power and place it had.
entries.2:32: God says there will never again be an old man in Eli's family. It means the family line will not enjoy the long, honored old age that a blessing would bring.
entries.2:33: One man from Eli's family will not be cut off, but his eyes will grow dim and his heart will grieve, and the rest of the family will die by the sword. It means judgment will bring ongoing sorrow, not just a single loss.
entries.2:34: God gives Eli a sign: his two sons Hophni and Phinehas will both die on the same day. It means God's warning is specific and certain, so it can be trusted as a real sign.
entries.2:35: God says he will raise up a faithful priest who will do what God wants, and God will give him a lasting family line to serve before his chosen one forever. It means God will replace corrupt leadership with someone who truly follows him.
entries.2:36: The remaining members of Eli's family will come and kneel before that faithful priest, asking for a bit of silver or bread and begging for a place among the priests just to have food. It means those who once had honor will end up humbled and dependent, showing how far they fall.
entries.3:1: God rarely spoke to people in those days, and young Samuel served God by helping the priest Eli. It reminds us that God can still speak even when things seem quiet.
entries.3:2: Eli was old and his eyesight was failing, so he was lying down to rest. It shows that even the leaders of God's people grow weak.
entries.3:3: The lamp in God's house was still lit and Samuel was sleeping near the ark, the special chest that stood for God's presence. God often speaks in ordinary, quiet moments.
entries.3:4: God called Samuel by name, and Samuel answered right away. God knows each person by name and invites us to respond.
entries.3:5: Samuel ran to Eli because he thought the old priest had called him, but Eli sent him back to bed. It shows how easy it is to mistake God's voice for someone else's.
entries.3:6: God called again and Samuel again went to Eli, who still said he had not called. God is patient and keeps calling even when we don't understand at first.
entries.3:7: Samuel did not yet know God personally, and God's word had not yet been revealed to him. Knowing about God is not the same as knowing him, and that knowledge can grow.
entries.3:8: After the third call, Eli realized it was God speaking to the boy. Sometimes we need someone older or wiser to help us recognize what God is doing.
entries.3:9: Eli told Samuel to answer the next call by saying he was listening as God's servant. We can prepare our hearts to listen and respond when God speaks.
entries.3:10: God came and called Samuel twice by name, and Samuel answered as Eli had taught him. God speaks personally, and we can answer him with open ears.
entries.3:11: God told Samuel he was about to do something in Israel so shocking that everyone who heard it would be stunned. God's judgment is real and should be taken seriously.
entries.3:12: God said he would carry out everything he had warned about Eli's family. God keeps his word, both his promises and his warnings.
entries.3:13: God was punishing Eli's family because his sons were cursing God and Eli did not stop them. Leaders are responsible for correcting serious wrong in those they oversee.
entries.3:14: God swore that no sacrifice could ever remove the guilt of Eli's family. Some choices have consequences that cannot be undone by religious rituals.
entries.3:15: Samuel stayed in bed until morning and was afraid to tell Eli what God had said. It is natural to fear delivering hard news, but honesty matters.
entries.3:16: Eli called Samuel his son, and Samuel answered him respectfully. A relationship of trust and respect makes hard conversations possible.
entries.3:17: Eli demanded to hear everything God said and warned Samuel not to hide anything. We should be willing to hear the whole truth, even the parts we don't like.
entries.3:18: Samuel told Eli everything, and Eli accepted it, saying God should do what seems right to him. Trusting God means accepting his will even when it is painful.
entries.3:19: As Samuel grew, God was with him and made everything he said come true. God backs up the words of those who faithfully serve him.
entries.3:20: Everyone in Israel, from one end of the land to the other, recognized Samuel as a true prophet of God. A faithful life earns trust and recognition over time.
entries.3:21: God continued to appear at Shiloh and gave Samuel his messages there. God keeps speaking to his people through those he has chosen.
entries.4:1: The Philistines gathered their army to fight Israel, and both sides set up camp facing each other. This sets the scene for a battle the Israelites were about to lose.
entries.4:2: The Philistines attacked, the fighting was fierce, and Israel was beaten, losing about four thousand soldiers. A defeat like this would have shaken the people's confidence.
entries.4:3: The Israelite leaders asked why God had let them lose, then decided to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, hoping it would protect them and give them victory. They treated the ark like a lucky charm instead of trusting God himself.
entries.4:4: The people sent for the ark, which was kept at Shiloh and was associated with God's presence, and Eli's two sons Hophni and Phinehas came with it. These sons were known for doing evil, so carrying the ark did not make them right with God.
entries.4:5: When the ark arrived at the camp, the Israelites shouted so loudly that the ground shook. They were confident the ark would save them.
entries.4:6: The Philistines heard the loud shouting and realized the ark of the Lord had been brought into the Israelite camp. They understood something unusual was happening.
entries.4:7: The Philistines were terrified and said God had come into the Israelite camp, and they feared disaster because nothing like this had happened before. They were afraid of the God of Israel.
entries.4:8: The Philistines asked who could save them from these mighty gods, remembering how those gods had struck the Egyptians with plagues in the wilderness. They were recalling Israel's history and feared the same power.
entries.4:9: The Philistines urged each other to be strong and fight bravely so they would not become servants of the Hebrews as the Hebrews had been to them. They chose courage over fear.
entries.4:10: The Philistines fought, Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent, with thirty thousand foot soldiers killed. It was a devastating loss for Israel.
entries.4:11: The ark of God was captured, and Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas were killed. The very things Israel trusted in were taken away.
entries.4:12: A man from Benjamin ran from the battle to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head as signs of grief. He came to bring terrible news.
entries.4:13: Eli was sitting by the road watching, worried about the ark of God, and when the man arrived and told the news, the whole town cried out loudly. Eli's greatest fear was losing the ark.
entries.4:14: Eli heard the noise and crying and asked what it meant, and the man hurried over to tell him. Eli was anxious to know what had happened.
entries.4:15: Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were so weak he could not see. He was old and blind, which made the news even harder for him.
entries.4:16: The man told Eli he had fled from the battle that day, and Eli asked him how things had gone. Eli was eager for news.
entries.4:17: The messenger reported that Israel had fled, many had died, Eli's two sons were dead, and the ark of God had been captured. This was the worst possible news for Eli.
entries.4:18: When Eli heard that the ark had been taken, he fell backward off his seat by the town gate, broke his neck, and died, since he was old and heavy; he had judged Israel for forty years. The loss of the ark hit him hardest.
entries.4:19: Phinehas's wife, who was pregnant and about to give birth, went into labor suddenly when she heard the ark was taken and her husband and father-in-law were dead. The shock brought on her delivery.
entries.4:20: As she was dying, the women attending her told her not to fear because she had given birth to a son, but she did not answer or pay attention. She was too overcome by grief to respond.
entries.4:21: She named the baby Ichabod, meaning the glory has gone from Israel, because the ark of God had been taken and because of her father-in-law and husband. The name was a sad reminder of what Israel had lost.
entries.4:22: She repeated that the glory had gone from Israel because the ark of God had been taken. For her, losing the ark meant losing God's presence and honor among the people.
entries.5:1: The Philistines had captured Israel's sacred chest, the ark, and carried it from the battlefield to their own city of Ashdod. It shows that winning a battle did not mean they had power over Israel's God.
entries.5:2: They placed the ark inside the temple of their god Dagon, setting it beside the idol as if Dagon had defeated Israel's God. They were treating the true God as one god among many.
entries.5:3: The next morning they found their idol Dagon fallen face down in front of the ark, like a servant bowing to a master. They set it back up, not realizing their god was being shown to be powerless.
entries.5:4: The following morning Dagon had fallen again, and this time its head and hands were broken off, leaving only the stump. This pictured their god as completely helpless before the God of Israel.
entries.5:5: Because of this, the priests of Dagon and visitors to the temple would not step on that doorway threshold. The story explains a custom that lasted long after.
entries.5:6: God brought a painful disease on the people of Ashdod and the surrounding area. The ark they thought was a trophy was actually bringing judgment on them.
entries.5:7: The people of Ashdod realized the ark was bringing trouble on them and their god, so they wanted it gone. They began to see that Israel's God was stronger than they had assumed.
entries.5:8: The Philistine rulers decided to move the ark to another city, Gath, hoping to escape the trouble. But moving the problem elsewhere did not solve it.
entries.5:9: Once the ark arrived in Gath, God's judgment struck that city too, and people of every age and rank broke out in disease. The trouble followed the ark wherever it went.
entries.5:10: The ark was then sent to Ekron, and the people there panicked, fearing it had been sent to kill them. They understood by now that the ark meant danger, not victory.
entries.5:11: The Philistine rulers finally agreed to send the ark back to Israel so it would stop causing death among them. Fear of death had spread through the whole city because God's hand was so heavy on them.
entries.5:12: Those who survived the disease were still suffering terribly, and the city's cry of distress rose up to heaven. The whole episode shows that no one can treat the living God lightly.
entries.6:1: God's sacred chest had been captured by Israel's enemies and stayed in their land for seven months. Even when God's people lose, God is still at work among those who don't know him.
entries.6:2: The Philistines called in their priests and fortune-tellers to ask how to get rid of the ark properly. When people are frightened by God's power, they often look for advice from the wrong sources.
entries.6:3: The advisers said to send the ark back with a gift to make up for wrong, and then they would be healed and understand why trouble had come. Admitting you were wrong and making things right is the first step toward peace.
entries.6:4: They were told to send five gold models of the tumors and five gold mice, one for each Philistine ruler, because the disease had hit everyone. The gift matched the harm done, showing they took the damage seriously.
entries.6:5: Making these gold models and honoring Israel's God might stop the sickness on them, their gods, and their land. Honoring God, even when you don't fully understand him, is wiser than ignoring him.
entries.6:6: They were warned not to be stubborn like Pharaoh, who only let Israel go after being humbled. Stubbornness against God only makes things harder for yourself in the end.
entries.6:7: They were told to build a new cart and hitch two cows that had never been used for work, then take their calves away from them. Setting up a test like this would show whether God or chance was behind the trouble.
entries.6:8: They were to put the ark and the gold gifts on the cart and send it off on its own. Leaving the outcome to God was a way of letting him show what he wanted.
entries.6:9: If the cart went toward Israel, they would know God had caused the disaster; if not, it was just bad luck. Watching what happens can help you see whether God is involved.
entries.6:10: The men did exactly as they were told, hitching the cows and penning up their calves. Obeying good advice, even when it seems strange, is often the right move.
entries.6:11: They loaded the ark of the Lord and the chest of gold gifts onto the cart. The gifts and the ark traveled together as a package back to Israel.
entries.6:12: The cows went straight down the road toward Beth-shemesh without turning aside, lowing as they went, and the Philistine rulers followed to the border. God can guide even animals to do his will, which is a comfort when you feel powerless.
entries.6:13: The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat when they looked up, saw the ark, and were thrilled. Seeing God's presence return brings real joy to those who have missed it.
entries.6:14: The cart stopped in Joshua's field by a large stone, and the people broke up the cart for firewood and sacrificed the cows to the Lord. Responding to God's arrival with worship is the right reaction.
entries.6:15: The Levites, the priests' helpers, took down the ark and the gold chest and set them on the big stone, and the people offered sacrifices and worshiped that day. God's people are to handle holy things with care and honor.
entries.6:16: The five Philistine rulers watched all this and then went home to Ekron that same day. Once they saw God's power at work, they knew to leave it alone.
entries.6:17: The gold tumors were a guilt offering, one for each of the five Philistine cities: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Each city's gift showed that every place had been affected and needed to make things right.
entries.6:18: The gold mice matched every Philistine town, both walled cities and open country, and the large stone where the ark was set down was still there when this was written. Remembering where God acted in the past helps later generations trust him.
entries.6:19: God struck down seventy men of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark, and the people mourned deeply. God is holy, and treating him casually has serious consequences even for his own people.
entries.6:20: The people asked who could stand before such a holy God and where the ark could go next. Realizing God's holiness makes us humble and careful about how we approach him.
entries.6:21: They sent word to the people of Kiriath-jearim to come and take the ark to their town. When you don't know how to handle something holy, it's wise to ask others who can help you honor God properly.
entries.7:1: The people moved the sacred chest to a man's house in a nearby town and set apart his son to guard it. It shows that God's presence was treated with serious respect and needed someone trustworthy to care for it.
entries.7:2: The chest stayed there about twenty years, and during that time the whole nation was grieving and looking for the Lord. Long seasons of waiting can still be times when people turn their hearts back to God.
entries.7:3: Samuel told the people that if they truly wanted to return to God, they had to throw out their false gods and serve only him. Real turning to God means removing the things that compete with him and trusting him to rescue you.
entries.7:4: The Israelites stopped worshiping the false gods Baal and Astarte and worshiped only the Lord. Obeying God's call means actually letting go of the old loyalties, not just saying we will.
entries.7:5: Samuel gathered all Israel at one place so he could pray to the Lord for them. It helps to come together and ask God's help through someone who prays for the whole group.
entries.7:6: The people fasted, poured out water as a sign of sorrow, and openly admitted they had sinned against the Lord, while Samuel led them. Honest confession and humility before God are the right response when we realize we have done wrong.
entries.7:7: When the Philistines heard Israel had gathered, they came to attack, and the Israelites were terrified. Doing the right thing can still bring trouble, and fear is a normal reaction when danger appears.
entries.7:8: The people begged Samuel to keep praying that God would rescue them from the Philistines. It is good to ask others to pray for us when we are afraid and need help.
entries.7:9: Samuel offered a whole lamb to the Lord and prayed for Israel, and God answered him. God listens when his people pray and responds to their need.
entries.7:10: While Samuel was still offering the sacrifice, the Philistines attacked, but God sent loud thunder that threw them into panic and they were defeated. God can rescue his people in ways no one expected, even in the middle of the crisis.
entries.7:11: The Israelites chased the Philistines from Mizpah and struck them down as far as Beth-car. When God gives the victory, his people still have to step out and do their part.
entries.7:12: Samuel set up a stone as a memorial and named it 'stone of help,' saying the Lord had helped them up to that point. Remembering God's past help builds trust for the future.
entries.7:13: The Philistines were defeated and did not invade Israel again, and God kept them down throughout Samuel's lifetime. God's help was not a one-time event but lasting protection for his people.
entries.7:14: The towns the Philistines had captured were returned to Israel, and there was peace with the Amorites too. God's rescue restored what had been lost and brought peace on every side.
entries.7:15: Samuel served as judge over Israel for the rest of his life. Faithful, steady service over many years is a real gift to God's people.
entries.7:16: Samuel traveled each year to several towns in turn to settle disputes and lead the people. Good leadership often means going to where people are rather than waiting for them to come to you.
entries.7:17: Samuel's home base was Ramah, where he judged Israel and built an altar to the Lord. Having a settled place of worship and service helps anchor a life of faith.
entries.8:1: Samuel was getting old, so he appointed his sons to serve as judges over Israel. It shows how leadership gets passed on, and it sets up the trouble that follows.
entries.8:2: Samuel's sons were named Joel and Abijah, and they served as judges in Beer-sheba. This tells us where they worked and who they were.
entries.8:3: Samuel's sons did not follow his example; they took bribes because they loved money and judged unfairly. It reminds us that good parents can have children who choose wrong.
entries.8:4: The elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah. The leaders of the people were bringing a serious concern to the man in charge.
entries.8:5: They told Samuel he was old and his sons were not like him, and they demanded a king to rule them like other nations have. They had a real problem, but their solution was to copy the nations around them.
entries.8:6: Samuel was upset by their request for a king, so he prayed to the Lord. It is good to bring our hurt and confusion to God instead of reacting on our own.
entries.8:7: God told Samuel to do what the people asked, because they were not rejecting Samuel but rejecting God as their king. The real issue was deeper than a leadership problem.
entries.8:8: God said the people had been turning away from him and worshiping other gods since he brought them out of Egypt, and now they were treating Samuel the same way. Their pattern of rejection went back a long way.
entries.8:9: God told Samuel to listen to the people but also to warn them clearly and describe what kind of king would rule over them. God wanted them to know the cost before they got what they asked for.
entries.8:10: Samuel told the people who wanted a king everything the Lord had said. He delivered God's message honestly, even though it was not what they wanted to hear.
entries.8:11: Samuel warned that a king would take their sons to serve in his army, as horsemen and chariot drivers running ahead of his chariots. Their families would pay a price for having a king.
entries.8:12: The king would appoint some of their sons as military officers and put others to work plowing his fields, harvesting his crops, and making weapons and chariots. Their sons' lives would be used for the king's purposes.
entries.8:13: The king would take their daughters to make perfumes, cook, and bake bread for him. Their daughters would be pulled into serving the royal household.
entries.8:14: He would take their best fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his own officials. Their best land and hard-won property would not be safe.
entries.8:15: He would take a tenth of their grain and grape harvest and give it to his servants. A king would tax what they worked to produce.
entries.8:16: He would take their male and female servants, and their best oxen and donkeys, and put them to his own work. Even their workers and animals would be conscripted.
entries.8:17: He would take a tenth of their flocks, and they themselves would become his servants. In the end, having a king would mean serving him, not just being led by him.
entries.8:18: When that day comes, they will cry out because of the king they chose, but the Lord will not answer them then. God was warning them that some choices cannot be easily undone.
entries.8:19: The people refused to listen to Samuel and insisted they wanted a king anyway. They were determined to get what they wanted, no matter the warning.
entries.8:20: They wanted to be like the other nations, with a king to judge them and lead them into battle. Their reason was about status and military security rather than trusting God.
entries.8:21: Samuel listened to everything the people said and reported it to the Lord. He kept the lines of communication open with God even in a hard situation.
entries.8:22: The Lord told Samuel to do as the people asked and give them a king, so Samuel sent everyone back to their towns. God allowed them to have what they demanded, and the story moved forward from there.
entries.9:1: This introduces Kish, a wealthy man from the tribe of Benjamin, and lists his family line. It sets the stage by showing that Saul came from a respected, well-off family.
entries.9:2: Kish had a son named Saul who stood out for his good looks and was a head taller than everyone else. The reader should see that Saul looked like an ideal leader on the outside.
entries.9:3: Saul's father's donkeys wandered off, so he told Saul to take a servant and go find them. An ordinary family problem becomes the start of something much bigger.
entries.9:4: Saul and the servant searched several regions but couldn't find the donkeys anywhere. Their unsuccessful search is quietly setting up a meeting they don't expect.
entries.9:5: When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul wanted to turn back so his father wouldn't worry about them instead of the donkeys. Saul shows concern for his father, but he's ready to give up the search.
entries.9:6: The servant suggested visiting a respected man of God in a nearby town, since everything he said came true, hoping he could help them. A practical suggestion puts Saul on the path to the prophet Samuel.
entries.9:7: Saul worried they had nothing to give the man of God since their bread was gone. He assumes a gift is needed to ask for help, which shows his ordinary, cautious thinking.
entries.9:8: The servant said he had a small piece of silver they could give the man of God in exchange for directions. Their modest resources show how ordinary this visit seemed at the time.
entries.9:9: This note explains that people used to call a prophet a "seer" when they went to ask God for guidance. It helps the reader understand the wording in this story.
entries.9:10: Saul agreed with the servant's plan, and they headed to the town where the man of God was. A simple decision moves the story toward an important meeting.
entries.9:11: On their way up to the town, they asked some young women fetching water whether the seer was there. This everyday scene shows they had no idea what was about to happen.
entries.9:12: The young women said he was just ahead and told them to hurry, because he had come for a sacrifice and feast that day. The timing shows God's quiet arrangement of events.
entries.9:13: They explained that the people were waiting for the seer to bless the sacrifice before eating, so Saul should go up right away. Everything was lined up for Saul to meet Samuel that very day.
entries.9:14: As Saul and the servant entered the town, Samuel happened to meet them on his way to the high place. What looks like a coincidence is really God bringing them together.
entries.9:15: The day before Saul arrived, God had already spoken to Samuel about what was coming. This shows the meeting was planned by God, not by chance.
entries.9:16: God told Samuel that the next day he would send a man from Benjamin to be anointed as ruler over Israel, who would rescue the people from the Philistines, because God had heard their cries. God was responding to his people's suffering by preparing a leader in advance.
entries.9:17: When Samuel saw Saul, God told him this was the man he had spoken about, the one who would rule over his people. Samuel now knew for certain who God had chosen.
entries.9:18: Saul approached Samuel at the town gate and politely asked him to point out the seer's house. Saul had no idea he was already talking to the very man he was looking for.
entries.9:19: Samuel told Saul that he was the seer and invited him to the feast, promising to send him off in the morning and tell him everything he wanted to know. Samuel treats Saul as an honored guest, hinting that something important is happening.
entries.9:20: Samuel told Saul not to worry about the donkeys, which had already been found three days earlier, and hinted that all of Israel's hopes were now focused on Saul and his family. Saul came looking for animals but was about to receive far more than he expected.
entries.9:21: Saul replied that he was from Benjamin, the smallest tribe, and from the least important family in it, so why would Samuel say such things to him. Saul seems genuinely humble, or at least surprised, by this sudden honor.
entries.9:22: Samuel brought Saul and his servant into the guest room and gave them the best seats among about thirty guests. Samuel publicly honored Saul before anyone else knew what was happening.
entries.9:23: Samuel told the cook to bring out the special portion he had set aside. The meal had been prepared in advance, showing that Samuel was already treating Saul as the chosen one.
entries.9:24: The cook brought the leg with the fat tail and set it before Saul, and Samuel said it had been kept for him for this moment, so Saul ate with Samuel that day. This special portion was a sign of honor, quietly confirming Saul's importance.
entries.9:25: After the meal they came down from the high place into the town, and Saul rested for the night. The day ends quietly after all the unexpected events.
entries.9:26: At dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof to get up so he could send him on his way, and the two of them went out together. Samuel personally accompanies Saul as he prepares to share God's message with him.
entries.9:27: As they walked down toward the edge of town, Samuel told Saul to send the servant ahead so he could give Saul a private message from God. What Saul thought was a simple trip is about to become a life-changing moment.
entries.10:1: Samuel poured oil on Saul's head and kissed him to show that God had chosen Saul to lead Israel and protect them from their enemies. This was a sign confirming God's call on Saul's life.
entries.10:2: Samuel told Saul that on his way home he would meet two men near Rachel's tomb who would tell him the lost donkeys had been found and that his father was now worried about him. This was the first sign that God was guiding Saul's steps.
entries.10:3: Saul would next meet three men going to worship at Bethel, each carrying something different for an offering. These details would confirm that Samuel's words were coming true.
entries.10:4: The men would greet Saul with a blessing and give him two loaves of bread, which he should accept. This was another sign that God was providing for him along the way.
entries.10:5: Saul would then arrive at Gibeah, where Philistine soldiers were stationed, and he would meet a group of prophets coming down from a worship site playing music and prophesying. This would be a striking and unusual sight.
entries.10:6: God's Spirit would come powerfully on Saul, and he would join the prophets in prophesying and be changed into a different person. This showed that God himself was equipping Saul for the task ahead.
entries.10:7: Once these signs happened, Saul should act on the opportunity given to him, trusting that God was with him. The signs were meant to give him confidence to step forward.
entries.10:8: Saul was to go ahead to Gilgal and wait seven days for Samuel, who would come to offer sacrifices and tell him what to do next. This tested Saul's obedience and patience in waiting on God's direction.
entries.10:9: As Saul left Samuel, God gave him a new heart, and all the signs Samuel predicted came true that same day. God was at work in Saul from the inside out.
entries.10:10: When Saul and his companion reached Gibeah, a group of prophets met him, and God's Spirit came on him so that he prophesied along with them. This confirmed God's presence and power in Saul's life.
entries.10:11: People who had known Saul before were amazed to see him prophesying among the prophets and asked each other what had happened to him. His transformation was so obvious that everyone noticed.
entries.10:12: Someone there asked who was responsible for these prophets, and the question became a common saying about Saul. The point was that God, not human connections, was the source of this change.
entries.10:13: After the prophesying ended, Saul went on to the house. The extraordinary moment passed and normal life continued.
entries.10:14: Saul's uncle asked him and his servant where they had been, and Saul explained they had been searching for the donkeys and had gone to Samuel when they couldn't find them. Saul gave a simple, honest account of their trip.
entries.10:15: The uncle wanted to know what Samuel had told them. He was curious about the details of their meeting with the prophet.
entries.10:16: Saul told his uncle only that the donkeys had been found, but he kept quiet about Samuel's words concerning the kingdom. Saul was modest or cautious about sharing the news of his calling.
entries.10:17: Samuel called the people of Israel together before the Lord at Mizpah. This was a public gathering to formally present the new king.
entries.10:18: Samuel reminded the people that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt and rescued them from all the nations that oppressed them. He was reminding them of God's faithfulness before addressing their request for a king.
entries.10:19: Samuel pointed out that the people had rejected God as their king by demanding a human king, even though God had saved them from all their troubles. He then told them to stand before the Lord by tribes so the king could be chosen.
entries.10:20: Samuel brought the tribes of Israel forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected. God was narrowing down the choice step by step.
entries.10:21: The family of Matri was chosen from Benjamin, and Saul son of Kish was selected from that family, but when they looked for him he could not be found. The chosen man was missing at the crucial moment.
entries.10:22: They asked the Lord if the man was there, and the answer came that he was hiding among the baggage. Saul was apparently overwhelmed or reluctant about being chosen.
entries.10:23: They hurried to bring Saul out, and when he stood among the people he was a head taller than everyone else. His impressive appearance matched what people expected in a king.
entries.10:24: Samuel asked the people if they saw the man the Lord had chosen, since no one else was like him, and the people shouted, "Long live the king!" The people enthusiastically accepted Saul as their king.
entries.10:25: Samuel explained the rules for how a king should rule, wrote them in a book, and placed it before the Lord, then sent everyone home. The king's authority was to be guided by God's written standards.
entries.10:26: Saul went home to Gibeah, and a group of fighting men whose hearts God had touched went with him. God provided loyal supporters for the new king.
entries.10:27: Some worthless men questioned how Saul could save them and showed him no respect by bringing him no gift. Not everyone accepted God's choice, and opposition appeared from the start.
entries.11:1: An enemy king named Nahash surrounded an Israelite town and offered a deal: surrender and serve him. It shows how God's people were vulnerable and needed a rescuer.
entries.11:2: Nahash's terms were cruel—he wanted to gouge out their right eyes to humiliate all Israel. It shows that some offers are traps meant to shame and harm you.
entries.11:3: The town elders asked for seven days to find help, and Nahash agreed. It shows they were buying time and hoping someone would come to their rescue.
entries.11:4: Messengers brought the news to Saul's hometown, and everyone wept. It shows how deeply the threat affected ordinary people.
entries.11:5: Saul was out working with his oxen when he heard the crying and asked why. It shows he was an ordinary farmer who got drawn into a crisis.
entries.11:6: When Saul heard the news, God's Spirit came on him powerfully and he became very angry. It shows God can use strong emotion to move someone to act against injustice.
entries.11:7: Saul cut up two oxen and sent the pieces everywhere, warning that anyone who didn't join would lose their oxen too. It shows he used a shocking sign to unite the people, and they responded in fear of the Lord.
entries.11:8: Saul gathered and counted the army at Bezek—300,000 from Israel and 30,000 from Judah. It shows how many people came together for the rescue.
entries.11:9: Saul sent word that the town would be saved by noon the next day, and the messengers brought the good news. It shows hope can lift people's spirits quickly.
entries.11:10: The men of Jabesh pretended to agree to surrender, telling the enemy to do whatever they liked tomorrow. It shows they were stalling while help was on the way.
entries.11:11: Saul split his army into three groups and attacked at dawn, defeating the enemy so completely that no two survivors were left together. It shows the rescue was total and decisive.
entries.11:12: The people wanted to kill those who had earlier doubted Saul's kingship. It shows how quickly a crowd can turn on its critics.
entries.11:13: Saul refused to execute anyone that day because the Lord had saved Israel. It shows mercy and credit given to God rather than revenge.
entries.11:14: Samuel called the people to go to Gilgal and formally confirm Saul as king. It shows a public step to make the kingdom official.
entries.11:15: At Gilgal the people made Saul king before the Lord, offered peace offerings, and celebrated with great joy. It shows a moment of unity and thanksgiving after the rescue.
entries.12:1: Samuel reminds the people that he did what they asked and gave them a king. It's a reminder that leaders should listen to the people they serve.
entries.12:2: Samuel points out that he is now old and the king is in place, and that the people have watched his life for years. It means our conduct over time is seen by others, so living honestly matters.
entries.12:3: Samuel invites anyone to accuse him if he ever cheated, stole, or treated someone unfairly, and promises to make it right. It means honest leaders should be willing to be checked and to repay any wrong.
entries.12:4: The people admit Samuel never cheated them, was never cruel, and never took anything from anyone. It shows that a good reputation comes from treating people fairly.
entries.12:5: Samuel calls God and the king to witness that the people found no wrong in him, and they agree. It means honesty can be confirmed openly, not just claimed.
entries.12:6: Samuel reminds them that God is the one who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought their ancestors out of Egypt. It means God is the real power behind Israel's history, not any human leader.
entries.12:7: Samuel asks the people to stand still while he lays out God's case and recounts the right things God has done for them and their ancestors. It means it's worth pausing to remember God's faithfulness.
entries.12:8: Samuel recalls how their ancestors cried out in Egypt and God sent Moses and Aaron to rescue them and bring them to their land. It means God hears people when they call to him in trouble.
entries.12:9: Samuel says the people forgot God, so he let their enemies like Sisera, the Philistines, and Moab defeat them. It means turning away from God leads to trouble.
entries.12:10: The people admitted their sin, stopped worshiping false gods, and asked God to rescue them, promising to serve him. It means honest confession and turning back to God is the right response to failure.
entries.12:11: Samuel reminds them that God sent leaders like Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel to rescue them from enemies on every side. It means God keeps providing help when his people need it.
entries.12:12: Samuel says that when the Ammonite king threatened them, they demanded a human king even though God was already their king. It means we often want visible security instead of trusting God.
entries.12:13: Samuel presents the king they chose, confirming that God allowed it. It means God can work with our choices even when they aren't his first plan.
entries.12:14: Samuel says that if they and their king fear God, listen to him, and stay faithful, things will go well. It means obedience brings blessing for both leaders and people.
entries.12:15: Samuel warns that if they disobey God, his hand will be against them and their king, just as it was against their ancestors. It means ignoring God brings consequences, even for kings.
entries.12:16: Samuel asks the people to stand still and watch something great God will do right in front of them. It means God still acts in ways people can see.
entries.12:17: Samuel says it's harvest time, when rain doesn't normally come, and God will send thunder and rain as a sign of how serious their sin was in asking for a king. It means God can use unusual signs to get our attention.
entries.12:18: Samuel prayed, God sent thunder and rain that day, and the people were afraid of God and of Samuel. It means God answers prayer and people take him seriously when they see his power.
entries.12:19: The people beg Samuel to pray for them so they won't die, admitting that asking for a king was another sin on top of the rest. It means we should ask others to pray for us when we realize we've done wrong.
entries.12:20: Samuel tells them not to be afraid, even though they did wrong, but to keep serving God with their whole heart instead of turning away. It means failure isn't the end; keep following God.
entries.12:21: Samuel warns them not to chase after false gods that can't help or save anyone. It means putting your trust in things that can't deliver leaves you empty.
entries.12:22: Samuel says God won't abandon his people because of his own reputation and because he chose to make them his own. It means God's commitment to his people rests on who he is, not on how good they are.
entries.12:23: Samuel says he would never stop praying for them or teaching them the right way, because not doing so would be sin. It means faithful leaders keep praying and teaching even when people fail.
entries.12:24: Samuel tells them to fear God, serve him sincerely, and remember the great things he has done. It means gratitude for God's past help should shape how we live now.
entries.12:25: Samuel warns that if they keep doing evil, they and their king will be swept away. It means stubbornly choosing wrong eventually brings ruin.
entries.13:1: This verse gives Saul's age when he became king and how long he had ruled, though the numbers are unclear in the ancient text. It simply marks the starting point of his reign.
entries.13:2: Saul picked 3,000 soldiers and split them between himself and his son Jonathan, sending everyone else home. He was building a small standing army rather than calling up all Israel.
entries.13:3: Jonathan attacked a Philistine outpost, which made the Philistines furious at Israel, and Saul had trumpets blown to rally the whole country. One bold move by Jonathan turned a standoff into a war.
entries.13:4: Word spread that Saul had struck the Philistines and that Israel was now hated by them, so the people gathered to Saul at Gilgal. The nation realized they were now committed to a fight.
entries.13:5: The Philistines assembled a massive army with thousands of chariots and horsemen, too many to count, and camped near Michmash. Israel was facing an overwhelming enemy.
entries.13:6: The Israelites saw how much danger they were in and hid in caves, rocks, and holes. Fear had scattered the army before the battle even began.
entries.13:7: Many people fled across the Jordan River, while Saul stayed at Gilgal with the rest trembling in fear. His army was shrinking and terrified.
entries.13:8: Saul waited seven days as Samuel had instructed, but Samuel didn't show up and the people began slipping away. Saul was under pressure and running out of time.
entries.13:9: Saul ordered the offerings brought and offered the burnt offering himself. He stepped into a role that wasn't his to take.
entries.13:10: Just as Saul finished the offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him. The timing made it clear Saul had acted too soon.
entries.13:11: Samuel asked Saul what he had done, and Saul blamed the people leaving, Samuel's delay, and the Philistines gathering. He explained his reasons rather than admitting fault.
entries.13:12: Saul said he feared the Philistines would attack before he had asked God for help, so he forced himself to offer the sacrifice. He acted out of fear and impatience.
entries.13:13: Samuel told Saul he had acted foolishly and disobeyed God's command, which could have secured his family's rule over Israel forever. His disobedience cost him something lasting.
entries.13:14: Samuel said Saul's kingdom would not continue, because God had already chosen a man after his own heart to lead his people. God replaced the king who wouldn't obey him.
entries.13:15: Samuel left Gilgal, and Saul counted the men still with him, only about 600. His army had shrunk from thousands to a small band.
entries.13:16: Saul, Jonathan, and their 600 men stayed at Geba while the Philistines camped at Michmash. The two sides were positioned close to each other.
entries.13:17: Three raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp in different directions. The enemy was spreading out to attack and raid the land.
entries.13:18: One party went toward Beth-horon and another toward the hill overlooking the valley of Zeboiim, near the desert. The raids covered several routes.
entries.13:19: There were no blacksmiths anywhere in Israel, because the Philistines didn't want the Hebrews making swords or spears. Israel was kept from arming itself.
entries.13:20: The Israelites had to go to the Philistines to get their plows, axes, and other tools sharpened. They depended on their enemies even for basic farm work.
entries.13:21: The charge was set for sharpening plows, blades, forks, axes, and ox goads. Even simple repairs came at a price.
entries.13:22: On the day of battle, none of Saul's and Jonathan's men had a sword or spear except the two of them. Israel went into battle almost unarmed.
entries.13:23: A Philistine force moved out to the narrow pass at Michmash. The enemy was taking position for the coming fight.
entries.14:1: Jonathan, Saul's son, decided to go over to the Philistine camp with his armor-bearer, but he kept it secret from his father. It shows that courage sometimes means stepping out without waiting for everyone's approval.
entries.14:2: Saul was staying at the edge of Geba under a tree with about six hundred soldiers. He was in a safe spot while his son was taking a risk.
entries.14:3: Ahijah the priest was there carrying the ephod, a special priestly object used to seek God's will, and nobody knew Jonathan had left. The leaders were unaware of what was happening.
entries.14:4: Jonathan's path to the Philistines went between two sharp rocky cliffs, one called Bozez and the other Seneh. The way forward was narrow and dangerous.
entries.14:5: One cliff stood on the north side facing Michmash and the other on the south side facing Geba. This describes the steep terrain Jonathan had to cross.
entries.14:6: Jonathan told his servant they would go against the Philistines, trusting that God can save whether by many or by few. It reminds us that God's power is not limited by our numbers.
entries.14:7: The servant told Jonathan to do whatever he had in mind and promised to stand with him completely. Loyal support like that makes brave decisions possible.
entries.14:8: Jonathan planned to let the Philistines see them first. He was testing the situation rather than rushing in blindly.
entries.14:9: If the Philistines told them to stay put, Jonathan would wait and not go up. He was willing to let the enemy's response guide his next step.
entries.14:10: If the Philistines invited them to come up, Jonathan would take that as a sign that God had given them victory. He was looking for God's direction in the circumstances.
entries.14:11: When the Philistines saw the two men, they mocked them as Hebrews crawling out of hiding. The enemy underestimated them.
entries.14:12: The Philistines challenged Jonathan and his servant to come up, and Jonathan took that as God's sign of victory. He trusted God's leading even when the odds looked absurd.
entries.14:13: Jonathan climbed up using his hands and feet with his servant behind him, and they struck down the Philistines. Their bold climb turned into a rout.
entries.14:14: In that first attack Jonathan and his servant killed about twenty men within a small patch of ground. A tiny force did real damage because God was with them.
entries.14:15: Panic spread through the Philistine camp and even the ground shook, causing great fear. God was at work behind the scenes, far beyond what two men could do.
entries.14:16: Saul's watchmen saw the Philistine army melting away and running in confusion. The enemy was collapsing on its own.
entries.14:17: Saul ordered a count of his troops and found that Jonathan and his servant were missing. He realized something had happened without his knowledge.
entries.14:18: Saul told the priest Ahijah to bring the ephod, the object used to seek God's guidance. He wanted to know what God would say about the situation.
entries.14:19: As the noise from the Philistine camp grew louder, Saul told the priest to stop and withdraw his hand. He cut the seeking short and rushed to act.
entries.14:20: Saul and his men joined the battle, and the Philistines were so confused that they turned their swords on each other. The chaos in the enemy camp worked in Israel's favor.
entries.14:21: Hebrews who had been serving with the Philistines switched sides and joined Saul and Jonathan. People often flock to the winning side once the tide turns.
entries.14:22: Israelites who had been hiding in the hills came out when they heard the Philistines were running, and they joined the pursuit. Fear turned into action once victory seemed near.
entries.14:23: The Lord rescued Israel that day, and the battle moved on to Beth-aven. The credit for the victory belonged to God, not to any one person.
entries.14:24: Saul made a serious mistake by putting the people under an oath not to eat until evening, so the troops went hungry all day. A rash rule from a leader can weaken everyone under him.
entries.14:25: There was honey on the ground in the fields, left by bees that had gone. Food was available right where the hungry soldiers were.
entries.14:26: No one dared touch the honey because they were afraid of Saul's curse. Fear of a leader's word kept them from what they needed.
entries.14:27: Jonathan had not heard about his father's oath, so he dipped his staff in the honey and ate, and he felt refreshed. He unknowingly broke a rule that was harming everyone.
entries.14:28: A soldier told Jonathan about his father's oath and pointed out that the people were exhausted. The rule was doing more harm than good.
entries.14:29: Jonathan said his father had brought trouble on the land, since a little honey had refreshed him. He saw clearly that the oath was a bad idea.
entries.14:30: Jonathan argued that if the soldiers had eaten freely from the enemy's supplies, the defeat of the Philistines would have been even greater. Withholding food weakened the army.
entries.14:31: Israel defeated the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon that day, but the soldiers were worn out from hunger. The victory came, yet the people paid a price for Saul's oath.
entries.14:32: The starving soldiers rushed on the captured animals and butchered them on the ground, eating the meat with the blood still in it. Hunger drove them to break a rule God had given about blood.
entries.14:33: Saul was told the people were sinning by eating meat with blood, and he ordered a large stone to be brought. He tried to correct the problem quickly.
entries.14:34: Saul told the people to bring their animals to him and butcher them properly on the stone so they would not sin by eating blood, and they did so that night. He was trying to bring order back to a hungry, chaotic camp.
entries.14:35: Saul built an altar to the Lord, the first one he had ever built. Even a flawed leader can turn toward God in the middle of a mess.
entries.14:36: Saul wanted to chase the Philistines all night and wipe them out, and the people agreed, but the priest suggested they ask God first. It was wise to seek God before acting.
entries.14:37: Saul asked God whether he should pursue the Philistines, but God gave no answer that day. Silence from God can be a sign that something is wrong.
entries.14:38: Saul gathered the leaders to find out who had sinned that day, since God was not answering. He assumed someone's wrongdoing was blocking God's guidance.
entries.14:39: Saul swore that even if the guilty one was his own son Jonathan, that person would die, but no one answered him. His oath was rash and dangerous.
entries.14:40: Saul had all Israel stand on one side and he and Jonathan stand on the other, and the people agreed to do whatever he thought best. The whole camp waited to see how the matter would be settled.
entries.14:41: Saul asks God to show who is guilty by using the sacred lots, and the answer points to Saul and Jonathan rather than the people. It shows that God can reveal hidden truth, even when we don't get an answer right away.
entries.14:42: Saul narrows the question down to himself and Jonathan, and the lot falls on Jonathan. It means the guilty person is finally identified, even though it turns out to be Saul's own son.
entries.14:43: Saul demands to know what Jonathan did, and Jonathan admits he tasted a little honey. It means Jonathan tells the simple truth, even knowing it could cost him his life.
entries.14:44: Saul swears that Jonathan must die for breaking the oath. It shows how a rash promise can push a father to do something terrible, and it warns us to be careful with the vows we make.
entries.14:45: The people refuse to let Jonathan die because he brought Israel a great victory with God's help. It means the people saw God's hand on Jonathan and stood up for him, and it shows that a foolish vow should not be carried out.
entries.14:46: Saul stops chasing the Philistines and goes home, and the Philistines return to their own land. It means the battle ends for now, but the enemy is still there and the conflict is not truly finished.
entries.14:47: Once Saul is established as king, he fights Israel's enemies on every side and wins. It means God gave Saul success in battle, but it also shows that his reign was defined by constant war.
entries.14:48: Saul fights bravely and defeats the Amalekites, bringing Israel safety from its attackers. It means Saul did real good for his people, showing he was a capable leader even with his flaws.
entries.14:49: This lists Saul's sons and daughters by name. It means we are being given a record of his family, which matters later in the story of Israel's kings.
entries.14:50: We learn the names of Saul's wife and his army commander, Abner, who was also his relative. It means Saul surrounded himself with family and trusted men to help him rule.
entries.14:51: This explains that Saul's father and Abner's father were brothers. It means Saul and his top general were cousins, showing how family ties held his kingdom together.
entries.14:52: Saul was at war with the Philistines his whole life, and he recruited every strong fighting man he could find. It means Saul built up his army out of need, but the constant war drained his reign and never brought lasting peace.
entries.15:1: God had chosen Saul and made him king through Samuel, so Saul owed God complete obedience. The reader should remember that being given a task by God means listening carefully to what he says.
entries.15:2: God remembers what the Amalekites did to Israel long ago and says he will now hold them accountable. It shows God does not forget injustice done to his people.
entries.15:3: God orders total destruction of the Amalekites and everything they own, with nothing spared. This is a harsh command in its setting, and it shows that God's judgment was to be carried out fully, not partially.
entries.15:4: Saul gathered and counted a large army of soldiers from Israel and Judah. He was preparing to carry out the mission God had given.
entries.15:5: Saul arrived near the Amalekite city and set up his position quietly in a valley. He was positioning himself for the attack.
entries.15:6: Saul warned the Kenites to leave so they would not be destroyed with the Amalekites, because they had been kind to Israel in the past. God's kindness is shown to those who showed kindness to his people.
entries.15:7: Saul attacked the Amalekites across a wide area stretching toward Egypt. He did begin the job God had given him.
entries.15:8: Saul captured King Agag alive and killed all the other Amalekite people. He did most of the task but kept the king alive.
entries.15:9: Saul and the people spared Agag and kept the best animals and valuables, destroying only what was worthless. They disobeyed God by deciding for themselves what to keep.
entries.15:10: God spoke to Samuel. God was about to tell Samuel his judgment on what Saul had done.
entries.15:11: God said he regretted making Saul king because Saul had turned away from him and disobeyed. Samuel was deeply grieved and prayed to God all night about it.
entries.15:12: Samuel got up early to find Saul and learned that Saul had gone to Carmel, set up a monument to himself, and then moved on to Gilgal. Saul was honoring himself rather than God.
entries.15:13: Saul greeted Samuel and claimed he had fully carried out God's command. He was either fooling himself or lying about his obedience.
entries.15:14: Samuel asked Saul what the bleating of sheep and lowing of oxen was, since those sounds proved the command had not been fully obeyed. Saul's claim was exposed by plain evidence.
entries.15:15: Saul blamed the people for keeping the best animals, saying they were meant as offerings to God, and claimed the rest was destroyed. He made excuses instead of admitting his disobedience.
entries.15:16: Samuel told Saul to stop talking and listen to what God had revealed to him that night. Saul agreed to hear it.
entries.15:17: Samuel reminded Saul that even though he saw himself as small, God had made him king over Israel. Saul had been given great honor and responsibility by God.
entries.15:18: God had sent Saul on a specific mission to completely destroy the sinful Amalekites. Saul knew exactly what God had asked of him.
entries.15:19: Samuel asked why Saul had disobeyed God and grabbed the plunder, doing evil in God's sight. Disobedience and greed went together in Saul's actions.
entries.15:20: Saul insisted he had obeyed God, claiming he had destroyed the Amalekites and only brought back their king. He kept denying the truth.
entries.15:21: Saul again blamed the people, saying they kept the best of the animals to sacrifice to God at Gilgal. He tried to make disobedience sound religious.
entries.15:22: Samuel said God cares far more about obeying him than about offerings and sacrifices. Listening to and obeying God matters more than religious rituals.
entries.15:23: Samuel compared rebellion against God to witchcraft and arrogance to idol worship, and said that because Saul rejected God's word, God had rejected him as king. Rejecting God's word is serious, and it has real consequences.
entries.15:24: Saul finally admitted his sin, saying he disobeyed God and Samuel because he was afraid of the people and did what they wanted. Fear of people led him to disobey God.
entries.15:25: Saul asked Samuel to forgive his sin and to come back with him to worship God. He wanted the relationship restored and the appearance of worship kept.
entries.15:26: Samuel refused to go back with Saul, saying that because Saul had rejected God's word, God had rejected him as king over Israel. The consequence of Saul's disobedience was firm.
entries.15:27: As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of his robe and it tore. This small event became a picture of what God was doing to Saul's kingdom.
entries.15:28: Samuel told Saul that God had torn the kingdom of Israel away from him that day and would give it to a neighbor who was better. Saul's kingship was ending because of his disobedience.
entries.15:29: Samuel said the eternal God of Israel does not lie or change his mind like a man does. God's word and purposes stand firm.
entries.15:30: Saul again admitted his sin but asked Samuel to honor him before the leaders and people and to come worship with him. He cared about his public reputation even after confessing.
entries.15:31: Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the Lord. Samuel did this, but it did not change God's judgment on Saul's kingship.
entries.15:32: Samuel had King Agag brought to him, and Agag came trembling, thinking the worst of death was behind him. He was hoping he would survive.
entries.15:33: Samuel told Agag that just as his sword had left women childless, so his own mother would be childless among women, and then Samuel executed him before the Lord at Gilgal. This completed the judgment Saul had failed to carry out.
entries.15:34: Samuel went home to Ramah, and Saul went to his house in Gibeah. The two men parted ways after this confrontation.
entries.15:35: Samuel never saw Saul again before Samuel died, though he grieved for him, and God no longer took pleasure in Saul being king over Israel. Saul's rejection by God was final, and Samuel carried sorrow over it.
entries.16:1: God tells Samuel to stop grieving over Saul, who is no longer king, and to go anoint a new king from Jesse's family. For the reader, it means God moves on to new plans and asks us to trust him instead of staying stuck in disappointment.
entries.16:2: Samuel is afraid Saul will kill him if he goes, so God gives him a safe cover story about making a sacrifice. This shows God understands our fears and gives practical help to move forward.
entries.16:3: God tells Samuel to invite Jesse to the sacrifice and promises to show him which son to anoint. For the reader, it means God guides step by step when we obey.
entries.16:4: Samuel goes to Bethlehem, and the town leaders are nervous, wondering if he comes with bad news. It shows that doing God's will can make others uneasy, but Samuel reassures them.
entries.16:5: Samuel says he comes in peace and invites Jesse and his sons to the sacrifice after they prepare themselves. For the reader, it means coming to God should involve getting ready and being included in what he is doing.
entries.16:6: Samuel sees Eliab and assumes he must be the chosen one because he looks impressive. For the reader, it's a warning that we often judge by appearance, but God sees differently.
entries.16:7: People judge by appearance; God looks at the heart. You are seen for who you are, not for how you look.
entries.16:8: Jesse brings his next son, but God has not chosen him either. For the reader, it means God's choice isn't based on birth order or human expectations.
entries.16:9: Jesse brings Shammah, and again Samuel says God has not chosen him. For the reader, it reinforces that God's selection doesn't follow our assumptions.
entries.16:10: All seven older sons pass by, and none is God's choice. For the reader, it means God may pass over the obvious candidates and choose someone unexpected.
entries.16:11: Samuel asks if there are more sons, and Jesse says the youngest is out tending sheep. For the reader, it shows God often calls people others overlook or consider too young or unimportant.
entries.16:12: David is brought in, and God tells Samuel to anoint him. For the reader, it means God confirms his choice, and outward appearance alone isn't the reason.
entries.16:13: Samuel anoints David in front of his brothers, and God's Spirit comes on David powerfully from that day. For the reader, it means God equips the person he calls with his Spirit.
entries.16:14: God's Spirit leaves Saul, and a troubling spirit from God torments him. For the reader, it's a sober warning that rejecting God can leave a person in spiritual distress.
entries.16:15: Saul's servants notice he is being troubled by an evil spirit from God. For the reader, it shows that others can see when someone is struggling spiritually.
entries.16:16: The servants suggest finding a skilled harp player to soothe Saul when the troubling spirit comes. For the reader, it means practical care and music can bring real relief in hard times.
entries.16:17: Saul agrees and orders them to find an expert musician. For the reader, it shows Saul is willing to accept help for his distress.
entries.16:18: A servant recommends David, describing him as a skilled player, brave, wise, good-looking, and with God's presence. For the reader, it means a good reputation built on real character and God's help opens doors.
entries.16:19: Saul sends messengers to Jesse asking for David, who is out with the sheep. For the reader, it shows God can lift someone from ordinary work into a significant role.
entries.16:20: Jesse sends David to Saul with bread, wine, and a goat as gifts. For the reader, it reflects generosity and respect when responding to a request.
entries.16:21: David comes to Saul, serves him, becomes dear to him, and is put in charge of his armor. For the reader, it means faithful service can earn trust and open a place in someone's life.
entries.16:22: Saul asks Jesse to let David stay because he is pleased with him. For the reader, it shows that good service and character make a person valued.
entries.16:23: Whenever the troubling spirit comes on Saul, David plays music, and Saul finds relief and the spirit leaves. For the reader, it means God can use simple gifts like music to bring comfort and healing.
entries.17:1: The Philistine army gathered for battle and set up camp in Judah. This sets the scene for a real conflict that is about to affect God's people.
entries.17:2: Saul and the Israelite army assembled and lined up in battle formation against the Philistines. Both sides are preparing for war.
entries.17:3: The two armies faced each other across a valley, each camped on a hillside. They were close but separated, waiting to see what would happen.
entries.17:4: A huge Philistine warrior named Goliath came out from the enemy camp. He was over nine feet tall, which would have been terrifying to see.
entries.17:5: Goliath wore a bronze helmet and a heavy bronze coat of armor. His equipment made him look unstoppable.
entries.17:6: He had bronze guards on his legs and a bronze javelin slung across his back. Every part of him was geared for battle.
entries.17:7: His spear was enormous, with a heavy iron tip, and a shield-bearer walked ahead of him. He was a walking weapon of war.
entries.17:8: Goliath shouted at Israel's army, mocking them and challenging them to send out one man to fight him. He was trying to intimidate them into submission.
entries.17:9: He proposed a deal: the winner's side would become servants of the loser's side. The whole nation's fate would rest on one fight.
entries.17:10: Goliath openly shamed Israel's army and demanded an opponent. He was daring anyone to face him.
entries.17:11: Saul and all the Israelites were shaken and terrified by Goliath's words. Fear had taken hold of the whole army.
entries.17:12: David is introduced as the son of Jesse, an old man from Bethlehem who had eight sons. This connects David to the story that follows.
entries.17:13: Jesse's three oldest sons had gone to fight with Saul's army. Their names are given here.
entries.17:14: David was the youngest, and his three oldest brothers were in the army. David was left behind.
entries.17:15: David went back and forth between Saul and his father's sheep in Bethlehem. He had responsibilities at home.
entries.17:16: Goliath came out every morning and evening for forty days to taunt Israel. The pressure on the army was relentless.
entries.17:17: Jesse told David to take grain and bread to his brothers at the camp. This was an ordinary errand that would put David in the middle of the crisis.
entries.17:18: David was also to take cheese to their commander and bring back news about his brothers. His father wanted to know how they were doing.
entries.17:19: Saul and the Israelite army were in the valley fighting the Philistines. The battle was still ongoing.
entries.17:20: David got up early, left the sheep with a keeper, and went to the camp as his father had told him. He arrived just as the army was going out to battle.
entries.17:21: Both armies were drawn up in battle formation facing each other. The tension was high.
entries.17:22: David left his supplies with the quartermaster and ran to find his brothers. He was eager to see them and learn what was happening.
entries.17:23: While David was talking with his brothers, Goliath came out and shouted his challenge, and David heard it. This is the moment David is confronted with the enemy's taunts.
entries.17:24: When the Israelites saw Goliath, they ran away in fear. The whole army was terrified of him.
entries.17:25: The Israelites talked about the great reward Saul had promised to anyone who defeated Goliath: wealth, marriage to the king's daughter, and freedom for his family. They were focused on the reward but still too afraid to act.
entries.17:26: David asked what reward would go to the man who killed this Philistine and removed Israel's shame, and he questioned who this uncircumcised man was to insult the armies of the living God. David saw the situation as a matter of God's honor.
entries.17:27: The people repeated the same answer about the reward for defeating Goliath. They confirmed what Saul had promised.
entries.17:28: David's oldest brother Eliab became angry and accused David of pride and of coming just to watch the battle. He misunderstood David's motives.
entries.17:29: David defended himself, saying he had only asked a question. He didn't understand why his brother was so angry.
entries.17:30: David turned to others and asked the same question, and they gave him the same answer. He was gathering information and confirming the reward.
entries.17:31: When Saul heard what David had said, he sent for him. David's words had gotten the king's attention.
